publication.title: Gaza after the ceasefire: what the Yellow Line is, and what the September 10–13 strikes show
publication.summary: Eleven months into the October 2025 ceasefire, Israel holds roughly half of Gaza east of the Yellow Line and keeps striking Hamas targets west of it. The IDF says it killed the Khan Younis Brigade commander on September 10, 2026, and hit a vehicle in Tel al-Hawa on September 13; Gaza medics say two died and 13 were wounded. Gaza's health ministry counts more than 1,330 killed since the truce.
publication.body:
Gaza is under a ceasefire that has not stopped Israeli strikes. This record explains the arrangement a new reader needs, the strikes of September 10–13, 2026, and the casualty counts on each side of the argument, with the source of every number.

What the ceasefire set. A US-backed agreement between Israel and Hamas was signed on October 9, 2025, and took effect on October 10, 2025. It halted large-scale fighting, secured the release of the remaining hostages, and had Israeli forces pull back to a demarcation line inside Gaza known as the Yellow Line, which was meant to be provisional pending later phases, including Hamas disarmament, a technocratic administration and an International Stabilization Force (ISF) under a Board of Peace chaired by President Trump. Phase two was announced in January 2026. As of February 2026, The Times of Israel reported that only 19 of more than 70 countries approached had expressed willingness to contribute to the ISF and that Hamas remained armed west of the line. In June 2026 PBS described progress as stalled over Hamas's refusal to disarm and Israel's continued military presence, with each side accusing the other of violations while saying the ceasefire remains in force.

What the Yellow Line is. It is the line Israeli forces withdrew to; Israel keeps direct control of the territory east of it, about 53 percent of the Strip according to Gisha, an Israeli human-rights organisation, and The Times of Israel. Defense Minister Israel Katz ordered it marked with yellow-painted concrete blocks on October 17, 2025; Gisha says the marking was never completed and that blocks have been moved westward at points. On December 17, 2025, IDF Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir called it "a new border line, a forward defensive line for the communities," which Gisha reads as contradicting its provisional status. The IDF says it operates east of the line "per the ceasefire agreement" and that Hamas has "systematically violated" the accord by rebuilding capabilities and attacking troops; in its Briefing Room for the week of September 6 it said troops had rendered more than 26 kilometers of tunnels inoperable east of the line. Separately, Gisha describes an "Orange Line" used by Israel's Coordination and Liaison Administration to restrict where international organisations may move without coordination, covering about 64 percent of Gaza after a March 8, 2026 update.

How the line works day to day. The IDF treats a Palestinian approaching or crossing eastward as a threat and has repeatedly said it fired on people who "crossed the Yellow Line" and "posed an immediate threat," labelling the incidents ceasefire violations; this site recorded two such IDF statements from northern Gaza on September 3, 2026. The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, drawing on IDF reporting, counted 29 IDF-reported ceasefire violations between August 19 and September 3. Gisha, citing UN documentation, says 224 Palestinians were killed east of or near the line between October 10, 2025 and February 27, 2026. OCHA's September 4, 2026 situation report notes an explosive munition detonating about 30 metres from a UN convoy crossing the Yellow Line in Rafah on August 27. Israel also carries out targeted strikes west of the line against people it identifies as Hamas operatives.

The strikes of September 10–13. Late on September 10, an Israeli Air Force strike in Khan Younis killed Muhammad Abdul Salam al-Yazouri, known as Abu al-Haitham, the commander of Hamas's Khan Younis Brigade, the IDF and Shin Bet announced on September 11. The IDF said he had been the brigade's deputy commander, its combat-support battalion commander and its intelligence chief, had "advanced dozens of attacks on troops" in recent months and was working to restore the brigade's capabilities; it said the same strike killed a company commander, Hudheifa Muammar, and an operative, Muhammad Bahjat Rashi, and that a separate strike killed Moamen Jabr al-Sayed Abu Labda, described as a Rafah Brigade sniper-cell commander. Hamas published a "martyr poster" for Yazouri on Telegram before the IDF statement, according to The Times of Israel; that is Hamas's acknowledgment of his death and rank. On the morning of September 13, a strike on a vehicle in the Tel al-Hawa neighbourhood of western Gaza City killed at least two people and wounded 13, medical staff and the Palestinian Red Crescent told Reuters and Haaretz; medics said the bodies were dismembered and asked the public for help identifying them. The IDF said the strike "targeted two Hamas operatives" and gave no further detail. The identities of the two dead, and whether they were the intended targets, are not established.

The counts. Gaza's Ministry of Health, as relayed in OCHA's September 4 situation report, counted 1,334 people killed and 4,429 injured between October 10, 2025 and September 2, 2026, with 31 killed in the week of August 26 to September 2; The Times of Israel on September 11 put the ministry's figures at more than 73,400 killed since October 7, 2023, and more than 1,330 since the ceasefire. The ministry does not distinguish combatants from civilians. The IDF does not publish a competing count of Palestinians killed since the ceasefire; it publishes named operatives it says it killed, eleven of them in the week of September 6. The Times of Israel reported in February that four Israeli soldiers had been killed since the pullback to the line. None of these figures has been independently reconciled.

What is not verified. Whether the September 13 dead were Hamas operatives; whether any of the Yellow Line shootings involved unarmed people, as Gisha and The Washington Post have reported for earlier cases; the current precise share of Gaza east of the line, which Israeli officials have described at 50 to 60 percent at various points in 2026; and the timetable for the ISF or any disarmament.

Assessment, ours. The Yellow Line has become the operative fact of the ceasefire: a line that Israel's chief of staff calls a border, that Hamas does not cross in force, and along which most post-ceasefire deaths occur. The September 10 strike shows Israel is still targeting Hamas's command echelon west of the line, and the September 13 strike shows the cost of that policy is carried in part by people whose identities are unknown at the time of the strike's announcement.

Still open / watch next: identification of the September 13 dead; the next OCHA situation report; any change in the IDF's stated violation count; movement on the ISF, disarmament or reconstruction; and any IDF or UN statement on the line's position.

Last checked: September 13, 2026.

publication.title: Reported claim: the Venice documentary "NAZA" shows Israel used AI to kill Gaza civilians by design
publication.summary: "NAZA", by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, won Venice's Special Jury Prize on September 12, 2026. It rests on 24 anonymous Israeli military and intelligence interviewees who describe AI-assisted target selection and rising permitted civilian-casualty thresholds. The IDF "categorically rejects" the allegations. What is documented, what is asserted and what cannot be checked are set out below.
publication.body:
What is established. "NAZA" is an 80-minute documentary directed by the Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, who won the 2025 Academy Award for "No Other Land". It premiered in the main competition of the 83rd Venice International Film Festival on September 10, 2026, and received a standing ovation that festival reporters timed at about 25 minutes. On September 12, 2026, the festival jury gave it the Special Jury Prize. The film is a British production made by The Guardian and James Wilson's JW Films, with Jonathan Glazer as executive producer; international sales are handled by MK2 Films, and screenings are scheduled for San Sebastián (September 18–26) and the New York Film Festival (September 25–October 12). The title is the IDF's Hebrew shorthand for "nezek agavi", collateral damage: the number of civilians a planner expects an airstrike to kill.

What the film claims. According to the filmmakers and the reviews published from Venice (Deadline, Variety, The Hollywood Reporter, Screen), the film is built on interviews with 24 Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers who spoke on condition of anonymity. They describe an AI-assisted targeting system, referred to as "Lavender", that drew on Gaza's monitored telecommunications to generate suspected-militant targets; permitted civilian-casualty thresholds per target that, the interviewees say, rose over the war until "20 becomes the norm" for a low-level suspect; strikes on family homes authorised with those expected casualties; and shootings in designated no-go zones near aid distribution sites. The directors say the mass killing was "systemic: not by accident, but by design". Reuters quoted one interviewee describing a phrase like "daddy's home" detected on a child's phone as sufficient to trigger a strike. These are the film's claims, carried by anonymous testimony; this desk has not seen the underlying interviews and cannot verify the identities, ranks, units or dates the interviewees cover.

What is documented from before the film. In April 2024 Abraham published, in +972 Magazine and Local Call with The Guardian, an investigation based on six anonymous intelligence sources describing "Lavender" and reporting that the system had marked some 37,000 Palestinians as suspected militants. The IDF's response at the time, quoted by JTA and The Guardian, said its analysts use information systems as tools, that it does not use an AI system that identifies operatives or predicts whether a person is a terrorist, that it assesses "expected military advantage and likely collateral damage" before every strike, and that it rejected "any policy to kill tens of thousands of people in their homes". The film extends that 2024 reporting from six sources to 24 and adds the collateral-damage thresholds and the aid-site zones. The Times of Israel notes that parts of the earlier reporting "have been challenged by the Israel Defense Forces".

The response. On September 11–12, 2026, the IDF said it "categorically rejects" the allegations, criticised the use of anonymous testimonies whose identities "cannot be verified", said claims about "national and military strategy" exceed what junior soldiers can know, and stated that "the selection and approval of Gaza strikes [were] made by human personnel only … and not by artificial intelligence". It repeated that it "tried to avoid killing civilians" and that Hamas embedded its operatives and infrastructure among the civilian population, and it rejects all accusations of genocide. Former prime minister Naftali Bennett called the film "a horrific blood libel against our sons and daughters". Abraham answered the military's criticism with: "It seems like an attempt to not face reality", and called the reporting "rigorous". This desk found no Foreign Ministry statement as of September 13, 2026.

How it is spreading, and by whom. Three distinct streams carry the film. First, the film's own campaign: The Guardian as producer, festival press, and the directors' acceptance remarks ("It's our country that is doing these crimes"). Second, outlets that convert the testimony into a settled finding: RT ran "Israel used AI to kill thousands of Palestinians in Gaza – documentary"; Al Jazeera filed its coverage under "Crimes Against Humanity"; the activist site Daily Kos headlined "the Gaza genocide"; the conspiracy site The People's Voice ran "Insanely fun video game: Israeli soldiers describe slaughtering thousands". Third, the counter-stream, which dismisses the film wholesale as "blood libel" without engaging the testimony. A figure of "up to 70,000 human targets" circulates in the second stream; this desk could not trace it to a verifiable statement in the film and the only figure with a documented origin is the 37,000 of the 2024 investigation. Do not repeat 70,000 as a fact.

Assessment (Lions of Zion). Legitimate criticism is not propaganda because it is severe, and testimony from serving or former soldiers is a recognised form of journalism whose anonymity is normal. Two things are nevertheless true at once. The film cannot be checked by an outside reader: the sources are anonymous, the thresholds are recollected rather than shown in documents, and the film does not publish the orders it describes. And the IDF's denial is a blanket institutional statement that does not engage the specific thresholds or dates, and the same institution's own inquiries in 2025–2026 have acknowledged serious failures elsewhere. The resolution state is therefore disputed, not refuted and not verified. The claim that AI selected targets without human approval is contradicted by the IDF and, notably, not what the 2024 reporting said either: the sources then described humans approving machine-generated lists quickly, which is a claim about oversight, not about autonomy. The claim that civilian deaths were budgeted into strikes on homes is a claim about proportionality thresholds, which only documents or a judicial process can settle.

What a reader can do. Separate three propositions when this film is cited: that an AI-assisted database existed and shaped target lists (reported by multiple sources since 2024, characterised differently by the IDF); that permitted civilian-casualty thresholds were set and rose (asserted by anonymous testimony, denied as policy); that killing was intentional by design (the film's conclusion, not a documented finding). Ask which of the three a post is actually claiming, and whether it cites the film, the 2024 reporting, or nothing.

Still open / watch next. Whether any interviewee goes on the record; whether the directors publish documents; whether the Military Advocate General or a court addresses the thresholds; the film's Israeli release; whether a Foreign Ministry or government statement follows Bennett's; and how the 70,000 figure propagates.

Last checked: September 13, 2026.

publication.title: Death threat against Charlotte Knobloch after the Saxony-Anhalt vote; Munich state-security police investigate
publication.summary: A witness found "Die AfD hat gewonnen, morgen hängen wir die Knobloch" painted on a bench and a bin in Munich's Englischer Garten on September 10, 2026. Munich police and the Bavarian prosecutor's antisemitism officer are investigating for incitement, threats and criminal damage. Knobloch, 93, cancelled one event. The same week, a woman wearing a Star of David was cut with a bottle in Berlin.
publication.body:
What happened. At about 1:10 p.m. on Thursday, September 10, 2026, a passer-by noticed white lettering on a park bench and a rubbish bin in the southern part of Munich's Englischer Garten, near Lerchenfeldstraße, Seeaustraße and the Hirschanger sports ground, and called the police. The Munich police headquarters (Polizeipräsidium München) said in its press report of September 11 that "a so far unknown perpetrator had applied a personal threat against a member of the Israelitische Kultusgemeinde in white lettering", and that Kriminalfachdezernat 4, the unit responsible for state-security offences, had taken over the investigation for threats (Bedrohung) and criminal damage (Sachbeschädigung). The Israelitische Kultusgemeinde München und Oberbayern confirmed that the person named was its president, Charlotte Knobloch, who is 93 and a Holocaust survivor. According to the Abendzeitung, the sentence read: "Die AfD hat gewonnen, morgen hängen wir die Knobloch" ("The AfD has won, tomorrow we hang Knobloch"), accompanied by a Star of David. A police spokesperson said the threat stood in explicit connection with the AfD's election result in Saxony-Anhalt. The message was painted, not carved, as some English-language summaries have put it.

Who is investigating. Beyond the police unit, the Generalstaatsanwaltschaft München has opened proceedings. Its antisemitism officer, senior prosecutor Andreas Franck, said the investigation covers incitement to hatred (Volksverhetzung), threats and criminal damage, and confirmed the Star of David in the graffiti. Police have asked anyone who saw something in that part of the park on September 10 to contact Kriminalfachdezernat 4 on 089 2910-0. No suspect had been named as of September 13, 2026.

Context. The Saxony-Anhalt state election on September 6, 2026 gave the AfD 43.8 percent, its highest result in any state election and just short of an absolute majority of seats; the party's state branch is classified by the state's constitutional-protection office as confirmed right-wing extremist. Knobloch said afterwards: "An diesem Tag fällt es mir schwer, meine Heimat noch wiederzuerkennen" and "Das macht mir Angst". In an interview with Stern published on August 19, 2026, she had said she sees "in vielen Bereichen keinen Unterschied mehr zur NSDAP, bevor diese an die Macht gekommen ist", and argued that Germany should at least examine a ban procedure against the AfD: she constantly hears why it should not be possible, she said, but "at least as important would be why it might be necessary".

Reactions. Bavaria's antisemitism commissioner Ludwig Spaenle said the threat "überschreitet jede Grenze", called it "mehr als ein Tabubruch" and said Germany stands at a crossroads. Knobloch cancelled her participation in an evening event on September 10 for security reasons. She said she would keep her Rosh Hashanah engagements, including the public shofar blowing on St.-Jakobs-Platz on Sunday, September 13, at which she was quoted in a community statement: "Der Klang des Widderhorns soll die Menschen wachrütteln." This desk could not confirm from the reports available whether she appeared in person. This desk found no statement from the Central Council of Jews in Germany specific to the threat as of September 13.

The same week in Berlin. In the early hours of Friday, September 11, 2026, at about 2:30 a.m., two unknown men accosted a 43-year-old woman on Torstraße in Berlin-Mitte over the Star of David pendant she was wearing, shouted antisemitic insults, and one of them attacked her with a broken glass bottle; she suffered several cuts to her hand while defending herself and was taken to hospital. The attackers fled. The Berlin police published the case as press release Nr. 1171 on September 12 and the state-security division of the Landeskriminalamt is investigating. (One English report dates the attack to Friday, September 12; the police release places it in the night to Friday, September 11.)

The trend. The Federal Association of RIAS reporting offices recorded 8,725 antisemitic incidents in Germany in 2025, a record, including 178 assaults and 257 threats; RIAS classified 68 percent as Israel-related. The Central Council's 2026 situation report says the permanent threat is pushing Jewish life out of public space and behind security measures. Both German incidents this week fall into categories RIAS counts separately: a threat against a named community leader, and a physical assault on a visibly Jewish person.

Resources. Munich police witness line 089 2910-0 (Kriminalfachdezernat 4). Incidents anywhere in Germany can be reported to RIAS at report-antisemitism.de, including anonymously and below the criminal threshold. The IKG München und Oberbayern (ikg-m.de) publishes its public events and security guidance.

Still open / watch next: identification of the Munich perpetrator; whether the Berlin attackers are identified; any Central Council or federal-government statement; whether the AfD state branch comments; and the RIAS Bavaria and RIAS Berlin quarterly tallies.

Last checked: September 13, 2026.

publication.title: Israel takes gold and silver at the 2026 iQFOiL World Championships: Steinberg wins, Kantor second, Peleg fourth
publication.summary: Tamar Steinberg, 20, won the women's title at the 2026 Musto iQFOiL World Championships in Weymouth and Portland, England, on September 12, 2026, with Olympic silver medallist Sharon Kantor second and Daniela Peleg fourth. Steinberg led from the first day, adding the world title to the European title she won in May. The results are published by the iQFOiL Class and the Israeli Olympic Committee.
publication.body:
Tamar Steinberg is the 2026 iQFOiL women's world champion. The Israeli windsurfer won the title on September 12, 2026, at the Musto iQFOiL World Championships hosted by the Weymouth and Portland National Sailing Academy on the south coast of England. Sharon Kantor, also of Israel, took silver, and Stella Bilger of Australia bronze. A third Israeli, Daniela Peleg, finished fourth. The Israeli Olympic Committee published the result the same day, and the iQFOiL Class, the international class association that runs the championship, confirmed the podium in its final-day report.

What was established, and by whom. The iQFOiL Class report of the final day describes a Medal Series in which Steinberg and Kantor, first and second in the qualification series, went straight to the Grand Final, each carrying one match point. Bilger and Peleg came through the quarter-final and semi-final to join them. Kantor led at the first mark of the first Grand Final race; Steinberg overtook her and won it, reaching the two match points needed for the title in a single race. Steinberg had opened the championship with four consecutive race wins and led the standings throughout the week, according to both the class association and the Israeli Olympic Committee. In the men's event, Israel's Tom Reuveni won his quarter-final but went out in a semi-final that was re-sailed after a starting-procedure error; Luuc van Opzeeland of the Netherlands took the men's title ahead of Noah Lyons of the United States and Johan Søe of Denmark.

The numbers differ slightly between sources. The official results portal for the event lists 179 competitors from 39 nations; the class association's own press material says 186 athletes from 41 nations. Both are cited here rather than reconciled. Racing ran across the week ending September 12, with the qualification series combining upwind sprint, sprint slalom and course racing before the single-day Medal Series.

Who the athletes are. Steinberg, aged 20 according to the Israeli Olympic Committee, won the 2026 iQFOiL Open European Championship in Portimão, Portugal, on May 23, 2026, and took silver at the previous World Championship; the Weymouth title completes a European and world double in one season, which the class association notes she shares with van Opzeeland this year. Kantor, 23, won Israel's first women's Olympic sailing medal with silver at Paris 2024 and was iQFOiL world champion in 2024. Her 2026 silver came after she started the week in 16th place in qualifying, according to the Israeli Olympic Committee.

Why it matters. iQFOiL is the Olympic windsurfing class, so its world championship is the top annual title in the discipline and a direct marker for Los Angeles 2028. Israel already holds both Paris 2024 windsurfing medals (Reuveni gold, Kantor silver), and putting three women in a four-boat world final shows a depth no other nation matched in this event.

What it does not show. A world title in 2026 does not decide Olympic selection; Israel's Olympic berth and the choice between Steinberg, Kantor, Peleg and Shahar Tibi will be settled by the national federation's own process closer to 2028. No prize money or ranking-points figures were published in the sources reviewed.

What comes next. The iQFOiL season continues with the regular World Cup series; the 2027 World Championship venue had not been announced in the sources reviewed at the time of writing. Last checked: September 13, 2026.

publication.title: Houthis hold Yemen's Red Sea coast and Perim island; 76,000 displaced, and shipping risk rises without a proven closure
publication.summary: By September 12, 2026 the Houthis held Mocha, Dhubab and Mayun/Perim island in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait after government forces withdrew. The UN migration agency counted 76,000 displaced since July. A Houthi projectile hit Saudi Arabia's Jazan region. Territorial control raises shipping risk; it does not by itself prove commercial passage has stopped.
publication.body:
The Houthi movement, also called Ansar Allah, held Yemen's entire Red Sea coastline south of Hodeidah by September 12, 2026, including the port city of Mocha, the coastal town of Dhubab and the island of Mayun, also called Perim, which sits in the narrowest part of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and divides its two shipping lanes. That is the established position as of September 13, 2026, drawn from statements by Yemen's internationally recognized government, the Houthis' own military spokesman and reporting by AP, NBC News, Euronews and CNN.

Chronology, as reported. On September 10, 2026, Houthi forces took Mocha, and Euronews reports that the Zuqar island group in the southern Red Sea was seized the same day by rocket fire and a boat-borne ground assault. On September 11, Yemen's government said its forces had withdrawn from Mayun/Perim and that the Houthis had also taken Dhubab, the coastal town facing the island; a local official quoted by Euronews said boats carrying Houthi fighters reached the island after the government pulled out the previous day. Euronews adds that the coastal village of Murad fell within the same 18 hours. AP, cited in this record's September 12 version, independently confirmed the capture of Mayun/Perim.

The Houthi position. On September 11, the Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said, in a statement carried by Middle East Eye and The Times of Israel, that "maritime navigation is safe for all companies except for Saudi vessels," and promised "escalation for escalation" against Saudi Arabia. The Houthis have declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia since July 2026, according to Al Jazeera. On September 12, Saudi Civil Defense said a projectile launched from Yemen landed in Al-Tuwal governorate in the Jazan region, wounding two people and damaging a mosque, several buildings and vehicles, as reported by Arab News and Gulf News. Earlier in the week, on September 8, Saudi authorities had reported 73 people wounded in Houthi attacks on civilian and energy sites, per AP and Al Jazeera.

The government side. Yemeni government forces spokesman Majed Abdullah al-Nazili said on September 12 that government forces struck Houthi vehicles and personnel on the Mocha–Dhubab road, about 11 kilometers from Mocha, according to Al Jazeera. The Houthis said Saudi Arabia carried out 64 airstrikes in Taiz, Hodeidah, Marib and al-Jawf, a figure this desk cannot verify. On September 13, Haaretz's live page reported three Saudi airstrikes in Hodeidah province. None of this reporting describes a recovery of Mocha, Dhubab or the island.

Why Mocha fell, according to CNN. A September 12 CNN report, relayed by The Jerusalem Post, quoted a Western source with knowledge of anti-Houthi operations saying the Yemeni battalions at Mocha were roughly 20 percent of their paper strength because rosters carried "ghost names" that drew salaries, and quoted a regional source saying no Saudi airstrike came on the day of the attack despite minute-by-minute updates. CNN also reported that CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper was in Saudi Arabia for coordination meetings that day. These are anonymous accounts of a failure whose responsibility is disputed among Yemeni, Saudi and US actors; they are reported here as claims.

The US position. NBC News and Axios, cited by The Times of Israel, reported that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called President Trump twice on September 10 to ask for US strikes on the Houthis and that Trump declined, agreeing instead to help with targeting and intelligence sharing. On September 12 in Dublin, Trump said the Houthis had "called us, and they don't want to fight with us." The US has been at war with Iran since February 28, 2026, according to AP.

Humanitarian record. The International Organization for Migration said on September 12 that at least 76,000 people have fled their homes since July, up from 46,000 a few days earlier and four times the previous week's total, with more than 70,000 displaced since the start of September. IOM's breakdown: about 8,300 households, roughly 50,000 people, from five districts of Taiz; about 2,819 households, roughly 17,000 people, from Lahj, mostly al-Mudharibah district; about 1,374 households, roughly 8,100 people, from the coastal Hodeidah districts of Hays and al-Khawkha; and 191 households in Aden. Euronews reported the UN migration agency had also counted more than 500 deaths in the offensive as of September 12; this desk has not seen that death figure in IOM's own release and treats it as reported.

What the territorial change does and does not establish. Control of Mayun/Perim and the facing coast gives the Houthis positions on both sides of the strait's eastern lane and removes the government's last coastal foothold there. It does not, on its own, show that ships are being stopped, that commercial passage has ceased, or that all vessels face the same restrictions. Saree's statement is a threat scoped to Saudi shipping, not evidence of interdiction. The Houthis have declared a Saudi blockade since July, and the strait matters more now because Saudi crude that would ordinarily leave through the Gulf has been routed to Yanbu on the Red Sea while the Strait of Hormuz is restricted; see the linked Hormuz and Iran-network records. Iranian support for the Houthis is documented in UN Panel of Experts reporting, but that relationship does not establish Tehran's command of this offensive.

What changed since September 12: the story moved from a single-island seizure to a completed Houthi hold on the coast, a first Houthi strike inside Saudi Arabia after the coastal push, a doubling of the displacement count to 76,000, and public accounts, still anonymous, of how the defense of Mocha collapsed.

Still open / watch next: any authenticated UKMTO or insurer advisory for the Bab al-Mandeb; vessel-movement data showing diversions or attacks; whether Saudi or government forces attempt to retake Dhubab or the island; whether the US changes its position on strikes; the next IOM displacement figure; and any independent casualty register.

Last checked: September 13, 2026.

publication.title: Hormuz: an Iranian cargo ship is hit off Qeshm, one dead, as Gulf ministers head to Oman without Bahrain
publication.summary: A vessel was struck by an unidentified projectile in the Strait of Hormuz overnight September 12–13, 2026; Iranian media say it was an Iranian cargo ship with one crew member killed. An Iranian source says the Iran–Oman understanding will not reopen the strait immediately. Bahrain will skip the September 14 Gulf–Iran meeting. CENTCOM says no ship passes its blockade unallowed.
publication.body:
The Strait of Hormuz remained a contested and restricted waterway on September 13, 2026, with a vessel struck by an unidentified projectile overnight, a US blockade of Iranian ports still in force, and a diplomatic track through Oman that Iran itself says will not reopen the strait immediately. This record collects what is established, who says it, and what remains unverified.

Background a new reader needs. The United States and Israel have been at war with Iran since February 28, 2026, according to AP. Iran has restricted passage through the strait since March, according to Al Jazeera, and the US Navy has enforced a blockade of Iranian ports; earlier in September CENTCOM said US forces struck Iranian crude carriers after attacks on US warships. Gulf News, citing CENTCOM, reported on September 12 that US forces had redirected 99 commercial vessels in the 60 days since resuming the blockade and that "ZERO ships have passed through the blockade without US forces allowing." The Times of Israel, citing the Financial Times and emails from the US Maritime Coordination Center, reported on September 12 that Washington had reduced to two daily windows the periods in which it offers air defense to tankers transiting the strait, after increased Iranian attacks on ships moving at night; ships are advised, not required, to use those windows. This desk has not seen the Maritime Coordination Center emails.

The overnight incident. At 9:37 p.m. Israel time on September 12, Iran's state news agency IRNA reported that two explosions were heard on Qeshm Island "coming from the direction of the sea," as carried by The Times of Israel. The UK Maritime Trade Operations office (UKMTO) then reported an incident timed at 23:00 UTC on September 12 in which a vessel transiting the strait was struck by an unknown projectile; a later UKMTO update said a fire had broken out and that local authorities were evacuating those on board, according to CNN, Arab News and The Times of Israel. On the morning of September 13, IRNA quoted the governor of Qeshm County as saying an Iranian commercial cargo vessel with a ten-member crew had been hit off Qeshm and Hengam islands, that one crew member was killed, and that the authorities had not yet identified the projectile; the governor blamed a "terrorist enemy." Iranian outlets differ on the wounded: The Times of Israel and The Jerusalem Post, citing state media, said three; AP and Haaretz, citing ISNA, said four. No US or CENTCOM statement on the strike had been reported by the time of this update. Whether the projectile was fired by US forces, by Iran's own air defenses, or by another party is not established.

The Oman track. On September 11, Iran's foreign ministry said Iran would meet Gulf states in Oman on Monday, September 14, to discuss the strait, per Arab News and Al Jazeera; the Oman Observer and Muscat Daily reported the venue as Salalah and said GCC foreign ministers and Iraq were expected, with the aim of endorsing a joint Oman–Iran route through the strait and notifying the International Maritime Organization. On September 12 an Iranian source told the semi-official Tasnim agency that the Iran–Oman understanding "does not provide for the immediate reopening" of the strait but sets terms for a possible reopening that depend on US concessions, and that Iran still seeks to collect fees from transiting ships, which Oman rejects, per The Times of Israel. Gulf News, citing Tasnim, reported that Iran says the strait will stay closed until Washington meets seven conditions. Bahrain announced through state media on September 12 that it would not attend any collective meeting with Iran until diplomatic relations, severed in 2016, are restored, and called for Hormuz to be open "without discrimination, fees or permits," per Al Jazeera and The Times of Israel. The Jerusalem Post, citing an Iranian official, reported that no signed agreement is expected on September 14.

The wider frame. The BRICS summit in New Delhi adopted a declaration on September 12 calling for "maximum restraint" in the Middle East, according to Arab News, The National and Business Recorder; the group includes China, Russia, India and Iran. Saudi Arabia shut its East-West crude pipeline on September 11 after drone attacks launched from Iraq, which removes, for now, the main bypass Saudi exporters had used to avoid Hormuz; and the Houthis completed a hold on Yemen's Red Sea coast at the Bab al-Mandeb on September 11–12. Those two developments are recorded in their own canonical stories; their relevance here is that the alternatives to Hormuz are themselves under pressure.

Assessment, ours. The evidence supports a narrow conclusion: some traffic moves under US-managed and Iranian-threatened conditions, the US blockade of Iranian ports is enforced, and Iran is trying to convert the crisis into a toll regime through Oman. It does not support "Hormuz has reopened," "Hormuz is fully closed," or an attribution of the September 12–13 strike.

What changed since September 12: a lethal strike on a vessel inside the strait with no claimed author; Iran's own statement that the Oman deal will not reopen the strait immediately; Bahrain's refusal; and CENTCOM's blockade figures.

Still open / watch next: attribution of the Qeshm strike and the ship's name; any UKMTO or CENTCOM follow-up; what the September 14 Salalah meeting produces and who attends; whether the toll demand survives; and any change to the two daily air-defense windows.

Last checked: September 13, 2026.

publication.title: Iraq finds the launchers, sacks a commander and shuts three Iran crossings; who ordered the Saudi pipeline strike is still unproven
publication.summary: Iraq says drone launchers used against Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline were found in Maysan near the Iranian border. It dismissed the province's commander, closed three crossings with Iran and accepted an Iranian request for a joint investigation. Trump says Iran was "probably" behind it. No group has claimed the attack; the Islamic Resistance in Iraq denies it.
publication.body:
Saudi Arabia's East-West crude oil pipeline was attacked by drones on the morning of Thursday, September 10, 2026, and shut down the next day; Iraq has since confirmed that the drones were launched from its territory and has begun to act on that finding. What is not established, as of September 13, 2026, is which organization ordered the attack and whether Iran directed it. This record separates the two.

What the Saudi government said. On September 11 the Saudi Foreign Ministry said several drones launched from Iraq targeted the East-West pipeline in the Riyadh and Madinah regions, causing injuries and damage, and that the Kingdom had chosen not to respond at this stage after Iraq's prime minister asked for the opportunity to prevent further attacks from Iraqi territory, while reserving "the right to take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty, security and critical facilities." The Saudi Energy Ministry said, in a statement carried by Gulf News and NBC News: "The East-West Pipeline in the Riyadh and Madinah regions was subjected to several attacks on Thursday morning. The pipeline was shut down as a precautionary measure, and the attacks resulted in several injuries." No deaths have been reported. Independent remote-sensing material — a Copernicus Sentinel-3 image of the smoke plume and NASA FIRMS thermal detections cited in public reporting — corroborates fires at the pump stations; it says nothing about who launched the drones. CNBC estimated the pipeline had been moving four to five million barrels a day to Yanbu on the Red Sea, and reported that crude closed the week above 100 dollars a barrel for the first time in months. The pipeline matters because it is the route Saudi exporters have used to avoid the restricted Strait of Hormuz.

What Iraq found and did. Iraq's Security Media Cell, in a statement carried by the state Iraqi News Agency on September 12 and reported by Arab News, said a security and intelligence task force had tracked down and seized the launch equipment; Arab News, citing security sources, located the launchers in the remote al-Tib area of Maysan province near the al-Shib crossing with Iran. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi's office announced on September 11–12 the dismissal of the Maysan operations commander; Asharq Al-Awsat reported that the provincial police chief was also removed and a group of security commanders placed under investigation. On September 12 the prime minister ordered three crossings with Iran closed, Shalamcheh in Basra, al-Shib in Maysan and Mandali in Diyala, which officials described as "part of an intelligence effort to track down the perpetrators and prevent their escape" and to hinder drone smuggling, according to The New Arab and Al Jazeera. The same day, the prime minister's military spokesman, Sabah al-Numan, said al-Zaidi had approved "Iran's request to conduct a joint investigation" into the launch platforms near the border, per The New Arab; al-Numan also stated Iraq's rejection of any aggression that threatens Saudi security. On September 13, Al Jazeera reported that Iraq had seized a drone-launching platform used in the attack; that report was seen in search results only.

Who is blamed, and by whom. President Trump, asked in Dublin on September 12, said of Iran, "I think they are, probably they are," without offering evidence, per CNN and The Times of Israel. The Islamic Resistance in Iraq, the umbrella name used by Iran-aligned Iraqi militias, denied involvement in a statement quoted by The New Arab, calling the strike "an honour that we do not claim." No group has claimed responsibility. Analysts quoted by CNBC and others note that Iran-aligned Iraqi groups have carried out similar drone attacks in the past; that is a pattern, not proof for this incident. This desk has seen no Iranian government statement accepting or denying responsibility.

What this establishes for the network assessment. Iraq's own findings now place the launch site in Maysan near the Iranian border, which is consistent with a launch by an Iraqi armed group and also consistent with cross-border movement of equipment; the joint Iraqi–Iranian investigation, requested by Tehran, will be run partly by the state most often accused. Launch geography is evidence about where, not about who ordered. Iran's relationships with Hezbollah, Hamas, the Houthis and Iraqi armed groups remain well documented through sanctions records, UN Panel of Experts reporting and intelligence assessments, and the IRGC-Quds Force has been the central instrument of many of them. An established support network is still not a shortcut around incident-level attribution, and evidence of shared alignment does not establish a single operational headquarters or an Iranian order for this strike.

Adjacent developments the reader should hold alongside this: the Houthis completed a hold on Yemen's Red Sea coast at the Bab al-Mandeb on September 11–12 and struck Saudi Arabia's Jazan region on September 12; a vessel was hit by an unidentified projectile in the Strait of Hormuz overnight September 12–13; and the BRICS summit, with Iran present, called on September 12 for "maximum restraint." Each is recorded in its own canonical story.

What changed since September 12: Iraq moved from "investigating" to naming a launch area, sacking commanders, closing crossings and accepting a joint probe with Iran; the US president assigned probable responsibility to Iran without evidence; and the main Iraqi militia umbrella denied the attack.

Still open / watch next: the findings of the Iraqi and joint investigations; arrests or charges naming a group; forensic evidence on the drones; any Saudi decision to respond; when the pipeline restarts; and whether any Iranian official comments.

Last checked: September 13, 2026.

publication.title: After the Ali al-Taher demolition: Aoun rules out new talks for now, strikes continue around Nabatieh, and the next round slips to October
publication.summary: Israel detonated the Ali al-Taher tunnel complex on September 11, 2026. On September 12 President Aoun went to Nabatieh and Zawtar al-Gharbiya and said there would be "no new negotiations with Israel at the moment"; a US official said the Rome round moves to October. Israeli strikes near Nabatieh al-Fawqa and Tel al-Dabsha followed on September 13. The IDF's account of the ridge remains its own.
publication.body:
The Ali al-Taher ridge, above Nabatieh in south Lebanon, is where the military and diplomatic tracks of the Israel–Lebanon front met this week. Israel says it has finished destroying a Hezbollah underground complex there; Lebanon's president went south the next day and said there would be no new negotiations for now; and Israeli strikes around Nabatieh continued into September 13, 2026. This record carries the whole sequence for a reader arriving now.

Background. A June 2026 framework, mediated by the United States, set out a process under which the Lebanese army would disarm Hezbollah in designated pilot zones while Israel withdrew from positions it holds in the south; Hezbollah has rejected direct talks with Israel, per Al Jazeera. Since late August the IDF has operated on and under Ali al-Taher. On September 3 it said troops had cleared two Hezbollah tunnel routes beneath the ridge and taken operational control above and below ground; on September 11 it said it had completed dismantling more than two kilometers of underground infrastructure, including what it described as a Badr Unit command complex, weapons storage and living quarters. Hezbollah launched explosive drones at IDF troops in the security zone on September 2, 4 and 5, according to the IDF Spokesperson's weekly Briefing Room, and the IDF answered with strikes it said hit weapons stores and command sites; Lebanon's health ministry reported three killed and 23 wounded in strikes on September 5. All of those IDF findings remain the military's own account; this desk has not surveyed the site.

September 11: the demolition. The IDF detonated the complex with about 1,100 tonnes of explosives, according to UPI and Al Jazeera, producing a tremor measured at magnitude 4.1 and felt across the surrounding area. In a Telegram statement quoted by UPI, the IDF said it found inside "dozens of Iranian-made rockets, missiles, and UAVs, as well as machine guns, dozens of anti-tank missiles, and hundreds of mines and explosive devices." Hezbollah has not commented on the demolition itself; in a statement on earlier strikes it accused Israel of escalating "aggression and crimes against Lebanon through killing, shelling, destruction, and the systematic demolition of homes and villages."

September 12: Aoun goes south; talks slip. President Joseph Aoun made an unannounced visit to Nabatieh, where he toured the government hospital, and then to Zawtar al-Gharbiya, one of the agreed withdrawal zones, where he inspected Lebanese army units within sight of Israeli positions, according to The Times of Israel and Asharq Al-Awsat. He said "there will be no new negotiations with Israel at the moment," and listed four national priorities: Israeli withdrawal, the return of prisoners, the return of the displaced, and reconstruction, pledging to "achieve an Israeli withdrawal and rebuild the area." The same day an unnamed US official said the next negotiating round, scheduled for this month in Rome, "will not be happening until October"; Al Jazeera reported the reasons given as the Jewish holidays, a Paris conference and UN General Assembly preparations. Instead, the Lebanese and Israeli ambassadors are to meet at the US State Department in the week of September 14 to discuss implementation of the June framework, per Al Jazeera and The Times of Israel. Also on September 12, heavy explosions were reported at al-Mansouri and heard in Tyre, and Israeli artillery shelled Douha, the outskirts of Kfar Rumman, Arnoun and Wadi al-Salouqi, according to Al Jazeera; The Jerusalem Post reported that the IDF announced strikes in southern Lebanon that day and that the Home Front Command warned residents of northern Israel to expect explosions and aircraft activity. Al Jazeera put the toll in the Nabatieh area over the previous two weeks at at least 29 killed, including 12 members of one family in an air raid on Kfar Rumman; that figure is Al Jazeera's compilation from Lebanese sources and has not been reconciled by this desk.

September 13: strikes near Nabatieh continue. Lebanon's National News Agency reported Israeli airstrikes near Nabatieh al-Fawqa and Tel al-Dabsha, with the area near al-Dabsha hill hit twice in under thirty minutes, and artillery fire around Zawtar al-Sharqiyah, according to The Times of Israel and Haaretz live pages, the latter also citing the Hezbollah-affiliated Al Mayadeen. No casualties were immediately reported and the IDF had not commented by the time of this update.

Assessment, ours. The demolition ends the tunnel phase of the ridge operation as Israel has defined it, but the political consequence is the sharper development: the Lebanese president has said publicly that negotiations are paused, the formal round has moved a month, and the only live diplomatic channel is an ambassador-level implementation meeting in Washington. Continued Israeli fire around Nabatieh while Aoun stands in Zawtar al-Gharbiya, a pilot withdrawal zone, is the tension the framework has to survive. Nothing in the September 12–13 record independently verifies the IDF's description of what was under the ridge.

What changed since September 12: the demolition and its inventory claim are on the record; Aoun's "no new negotiations at the moment" is his exact position; the Rome round is confirmed as October; the September 12 shelling and September 13 strikes near Nabatieh al-Fawqa and Tel al-Dabsha have been added; the two-week toll figure is recorded with its source.

Still open / watch next: a dated October round; the outcome of the ambassadors' State Department meeting; any IDF statement on the September 13 strikes; whether Hezbollah resumes drone attacks on troops in the security zone; independently documented site evidence at Ali al-Taher; a reconciled casualty register for Nabatieh district.

Last checked: September 13, 2026.

publication.title: Anthropic reports Iranian propaganda operations using AI to conceal state origins
publication.summary: Anthropic's "Detecting and countering misuse of AI: September 2026" names three Iranian state-aligned propaganda bodies that used Claude to plan "soft war" campaigns in six languages, voice an IRGC spokesperson and attribute false claims to CSIS, Brookings and RAND; separate Iran-linked accounts built U.S. Navy targeting handbooks and profiled Israelis and diaspora Jews. Anthropic is the only source; no Iranian rebuttal has appeared.
publication.body:
What the report is. On September 10–11, 2026, Anthropic published "Detecting and countering misuse of AI: September 2026", a threat-intelligence report covering activity it disrupted between December 2025 and August 2026 across seven harm areas: cyber operations, influence operations, surveillance, scams and fraud, biological misuse, conventional-weapons development and illicit model distillation. The report and its PDF are the primary sources for everything below; Lions of Zion has not examined the underlying account data, and the descriptions are Anthropic's.

The three Iranian propaganda accounts. Anthropic says it identified and removed three accounts linked to Iranian state propaganda institutions: the Islamic Culture and Communications Organization, which sits under the Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance; the Islamic Propaganda Office of Khorasan Razavi; and the Islamic Propaganda Organization's Bina Cultural Observatory. According to the report, operators described their work as "soft war" or "cognitive warfare" aimed at audiences inside and outside Iran, and used Claude to build campaign plans, doctrine manuals, persona systems, target databases and ministerial planning documentation, and to convert official government intelligence bulletins into tailored material in Farsi, Arabic, Urdu, Malay, Spanish and English, with a broader plan covering 20 languages. Distribution, per Anthropic, ran across X, Instagram, Telegram, TikTok and YouTube and the domestic Iranian apps Eitaa, Bale and Rubika. Two specifics matter for readers of this desk. An account tied to the Bina Cultural Observatory generated messaging "in the official voice of an IRGC spokesperson". And during the 2026 U.S.–Israel–Iran war the network attributed fabricated claims to Western research institutions, naming CSIS, Brookings and RAND, so that state messaging would read as independent analysis. The report also describes target databases naming international officials and Iranian opposition figures, and counter-narrative content aimed at the Bahá'í community. RFE/RL reports that the Islamic Culture and Communications Organization account was also used to "complete organizational plans" for the July 2026 state funeral of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Anthropic rated the operation at category three on its Breakout Scale, meaning the content spread across multiple platforms, and says it banned the accounts and shared indicators with industry and research partners. Attribution, the company says, relied on account information, institutional references and public-source corroboration rather than shared opinions alone.

Other Iran-linked cases in the same report. A separate Iran-nexus actor used Claude to compile "targeting handbooks" against U.S. naval forces: a Python-based system gathered names of U.S. personnel from captions on public military photographs, ship and aircraft transponder identifiers, commercial satellite-imagery query scripts and naval-tracking websites, and researched vulnerabilities in shipboard systems including VSAT terminals and industrial control products. Anthropic says it banned that account, built detections and shared the intelligence with government authorities. Another account built an automated open-source intelligence tool profiling hundreds of individuals in Israel and Jewish diaspora communities, and used Claude to modify malware and build an obfuscation pipeline. The surveillance cases include components combining licence-plate recognition with mobile interception, a malicious Firefox extension harvesting social-media identities, and phishing pages built to activate only from Iranian IP addresses. The report is not one-directional: RFE/RL notes it also documents an exiled opposition (MEK-linked) operation that scraped more than 500 channels to profile people inside Iran. Reporting by Al-Monitor and Iran International summarises the same cases; those pieces rely on the report and are not independent corroboration.

What this does and does not establish. These are one company's findings about its own platform. Removing accounts stops access to one service; it does not show that the named institutions stopped operating, that their content reached many people, or that audiences were persuaded. Anthropic reports "some dissemination beyond Claude" and a multi-platform breakout rating, not audience figures. Independently, Recorded Future's research on Iran's 2026 conflict operations describes AI as a force multiplier for speed, visual quality and cultural fit of propaganda, naming networks such as Storm-2035 and "Attack Alarm"; that corroborates the pattern, not these specific accounts. Meta's adversarial-threat reporting for 2026 continues to list Iran among the three leading sources of foreign influence operations.

Responses. Al-Monitor asked Iran's Foreign Ministry for comment on September 11; none was reported. As of September 13, 2026, this desk found no Iranian state-media rebuttal, no statement from any of the three institutions, and no companion takedown announced by another AI company or platform. Context that shapes how the report is received: the Pentagon severed ties with Anthropic in March 2026 after a dispute over usage terms, which Navy Times notes in its coverage.

The practical lesson. The distinctive technique here is attribution laundering: state messaging voiced as a spokesperson, then re-voiced as a think tank. Similar language across outlets cannot by itself identify a controller. Trace the first attributable source; when a post cites CSIS, Brookings or RAND, open the institution's own site and find the report; check whether apparently separate outlets cite each other; and look for an authenticated organisational link before calling a campaign coordinated.

Still open / watch next: any independent replication by platform trust-and-safety teams or researchers; responses from the named institutions; whether the fabricated think-tank attributions can be located in the wild and dated; and follow-on reporting on the Navy-targeting actor from U.S. authorities.

Last checked: September 13, 2026.

publication.summary: Video-game clips, AI-generated video and recycled footage from earlier wars keep circulating as real strike footage in the 2026 conflict. This record now carries a dated case list from Full Fact, PolitiFact, Poynter, Lead Stories, AFP and Fact Crescendo, plus a September 2026 detection of a recycled AI clip presented as an Iranian strike on Khamis Mushait.
publication.body:
A recurring pattern of fabricated and recycled war footage has circulated on social media throughout the 2026 conflict between Israel, the United States and Iran and its allied fronts in Lebanon, Yemen and the Gulf. It is worth documenting as a pattern rather than as single incidents, because the same three techniques keep reappearing, and because a charged news cycle is exactly when viewers stop checking.

The first technique is video-game footage relabelled as combat video. Clips recorded in the military simulators ARMA 3 and War Thunder have circulated on TikTok and X captioned as real strikes, to the point that the Israeli military has publicly said specific viral clips were fake. Reporting on the pattern has linked at least some of the distribution to networks associated with Russian influence operations; this desk does not assert one coordinated campaign behind all of it.

The second technique is AI-generated video and imagery. A synthetic video claiming to show an Iranian strike on Israeli military headquarters was assessed by detection researchers as roughly 93 percent likely to be AI-generated, on physical inconsistencies and a building that does not match the real one. Poynter's March 4, 2026 review found three of four clips in one viral compilation of "Iranian bases under attack" to be AI-made, with warped door frames and unnatural movement, and only one clip real. Lead Stories showed on March 4, 2026 that an image of the U.S. embassy in Saudi Arabia "on fire" carried Google's SynthID watermark. Full Fact's March 13, 2026 overview lists AI-altered images of the Burj Khalifa burning, of the USS Abraham Lincoln on fire and of a B-2 bomber "shot down by Iran".

The third technique is recycled footage. Full Fact and PolitiFact traced a "THIS IS TEL AVIV. THANK YOU IRAN!" explosion clip to the 2015 Tianjin chemical-warehouse blast; a clip of a "US airbase in Saudi Arabia burnt to ashes" to an earlier fire after an Israeli strike in Yemen; and "Dubai strike" clips to a 2015 apartment fire and 2024 missile footage. PolitiFact showed on April 20, 2026 that a video sold as a U.S. strike on an Iranian cargo ship near Hormuz was the June 2025 collision of two tankers. Fact Crescendo on April 9, 2026 traced an "Israeli missile attack on Lebanon" clip to older footage. AFP Fact Check has separately traced clips of "recent Beirut strikes" to Israel's October 2024 bombing of the city and clips of "the 2026 war in Tel Aviv" to the June 2025 Iranian missile barrage, identifying one by an AFP videographer's own June 22, 2025 footage.

The September 2026 example. During the September 10–13 escalation in Yemen, the Gulf and Lebanon, a clip presented on X as an Iranian missile hitting Khamis Mushait in Saudi Arabia was flagged by the detection vendor UncovAI as probably AI-generated (a 76 percent score) and, by reverse search, as having appeared online about six months earlier attached to a different story. This is a vendor detection, not a fact-checker's verdict; it is cited here because it shows the mechanism, an old synthetic clip re-captioned for a real event, rather than as a settled finding. This desk found no top-tier fact-check dated September 11–13 for the Hormuz, Yemen or Lebanon events; that absence is recorded, not read as an absence of fakes.

What unites the three techniques is not central coordination. What can be said is that verified instances of each exist in this information environment, and that part of the game-footage distribution has been linked by researchers to Russian-associated networks.

What a reader can do. Treat any dramatic, uncaptioned strike video with default scepticism until a named military source or a wire service confirms it. Reverse-search a frame; if the same clip sits on an older story, it is not new. Look for the tells fact-checkers list: warped edges, impossible fire behaviour, buildings that do not match maps, stylised smoke. Remember that a real event (the Saudi pipeline fires of September 10–11, for instance) attracts fake footage precisely because it is real. AI-detection tools are imperfect, and a score is a prompt to check, not a verdict.

Last checked: September 13, 2026.

publication.body:
This record preserves two IDF statements from September 3, 2026. In the morning, the IDF said a man crossed the Yellow Line in northern Gaza, approached troops "in a manner that posed an immediate threat" and was killed; it called the crossing a ceasefire violation. Later that day it said two armed men crossed the line and were killed in the same circumstances. Both accounts are the IDF's; no independent account or identification was published.

The Yellow Line is the line inside Gaza to which Israeli forces withdrew under the ceasefire that took effect on October 10, 2025; Israel controls the territory east of it and treats eastward crossings as threats. Such incidents are the most frequent cause of deaths since the ceasefire, per UN documentation cited by Gisha.

The story continues in "Gaza after the ceasefire: what the Yellow Line is, and what the September 10–13 strikes show" (canonicalStoryId gaza-yellow-line-operations-2026-09), which explains the arrangement, the counts on each side, and the strikes of September 10 and 13, 2026.

Resolution state at closure: unresolved as to any formal forced-removal policy; verified as to the fact that Israeli ministers have publicly advocated large-scale "voluntary" migration.

The substantive assessment of the Gaza-migration claim, including the distinction between ministerial advocacy, a proposal, a formal decision and implementation, and the point that the label "voluntary" does not settle consent under the Fourth Geneva Convention, continues in the canonical record "Reported claim: Gaza migration proposals: ministerial advocacy is verified; forced-transfer implementation is not" (publicId reported-claim-claims-that-israeli-government-pl-nos0i). This record assessed a Reuters account of September 3–4, 2026: that Iran had warned the United States, via a third party, against an Israeli offensive on the Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon; that more than a dozen IRGC personnel were inside with Hezbollah; and that, under U.S. pressure, Israel had "put off" storming the ridge. Reuters could not independently confirm the situation on the ridge and a White House official rejected the characterisation of pressure. Within hours the IDF said it had already cleared Hezbollah's underground infrastructure at Ali al-Taher after weeks of operations and that neutralisation continued, a timeline that undercut the same-day "postponed assault" frame. Resolution state at closure: disputed. Whether IRGC personnel were present at any point during the siege, and the exact content of any Iranian message, remain unknown.

The Ali al-Taher story, including the subsequent clearance announcements, the state of Israel's declared security zone and the Israel–Lebanon talks now slipping to October, continues in "Aoun visits south Lebanon as next Israel-Lebanon talks slip to October" (publicId israel-says-it-has-cleared-hezbollah-s-ali-al-ta-6rr6p).
